case_study_insert.main_stem: Coral Bay Swimwear (CBS) is a partnership in the coastal swimwear retail sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2011 by Isla Corbin, the business sells swimwear through a Cornwall shop and a growing e-commerce channel and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. CBS plans to invest $180,000 in a new e-commerce website and photography studio, financed by $90,000 of trade credit from fabric suppliers and $90,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $98,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and currently produces 14,000 units a year. CBS faces two problems: fabric waste has reached 11.2% and delivery times are lengthening.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q2 2025: The Cornwall workshop cut 7,800 swimwear units, with fabric waste at 11.2% of material used, down from 14.6% a year earlier. Defects found at final inspection fell from 5.1% to 2.8%. Customer complaints dropped from 27 to 12 a month. Online orders shipped in 5.4 days on average. A survey of 450 beachwear customers found 66% prefer sustainably made swimwear and 57% would pay $3 more for it. Two of 30 staff have not completed quality-control training; external courses cost $640 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Coral Bay Swimwear as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.50% to 4.00%, increasing borrowing costs generally. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.40 to $14.23 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Synthetic fabric and elastic input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while seaside tourism consumer spending rose 3.9% in the same period.

questions.question_text: CBS is funding part of its $180,000 expansion with $90,000 of trade credit from fabric suppliers. Explain two advantages for CBS of using trade credit rather than spending its retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Trade credit lets CBS obtain fabric now and pay later, preserving the $90,000 of retained profit as a cash buffer against fixed costs of $98,000 a year. That liquidity is valuable when delivery times are lengthening and 11.2% of fabric is wasted, because the partnership can still buy replacement materials without immediately drawing down its own funds.

Point 2: Supplier credit is flexible and usually interest-free in the short term, unlike a bank loan, so it does not add a fixed repayment commitment alongside the $180,000 website and studio investment. Keeping the $90,000 retained profit untouched also gives Isla Corbin's partnership room to fund quality-control training at $640 per person, helping reduce the 2.8% defect rate without seeking outside finance.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to CBS's trade credit, retained profit and expansion.

questions.question_text: CBS is launching a new sustainable swimwear range. Consider sponsorship of a local surf competition, print advertising in a holiday magazine, or social-media influencer marketing. Which should CBS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local surf competition sponsorship: Sponsoring a surf event puts the brand directly in front of coastal swimwear buyers and builds local credibility for a Cornwall-based partnership. It is relatively low-cost and generates photographs for the new e-commerce website. However, its reach is geographically narrow; a website can sell nationally, so a single local event may not generate enough orders to utilise 14,000 units of capacity, and impact is concentrated in one weekend.

Holiday magazine print advertising: Print reaches holidaymakers planning beach trips and suits a seasonal product, with a tangible, credible presence. Lead times are long, however, and there is no direct link from the page to the website, so conversion is hard to measure. For a small 30-staff firm investing $180,000 in a new website, a magazine campaign that cannot be tracked is difficult to justify against fixed costs of $98,000.

Social-media influencer marketing: The insert shows 66% of surveyed beachwear customers prefer sustainably made swimwear and 57% would pay $3 more for it. Influencers can demonstrate the sustainable range visually, link straight to the e-commerce site, and are measurable. They reach a national audience far beyond a local event and can be selected for beach and lifestyle credibility, though results depend on choosing credible partners and can take time to build.

Recommendation: CBS should choose social-media influencer marketing. It targets the sustainability-conscious segment revealed by the survey, is measurable, and drives traffic to the new website nationally. Local surf sponsorship is rejected as too narrow for an online channel, and magazine print is rejected because it is slow, untrackable and costly for a partnership with $98,000 fixed costs. CBS can retain a small local event presence as supporting activity, not as the main launch channel.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to CBS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to CBS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to CBS with a justified recommendation explaining why local sponsorship and print are rejected.

questions.question_text: CBS's fabric waste has reached 11.2%. Explain two benefits for CBS of introducing quality circles to involve staff in reducing this waste.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quality circles let the 30 staff meet regularly to identify why 11.2% of fabric is wasted, sharing practical knowledge of cutting patterns and machine settings. Because the people closest to the work propose solutions, suggestions are more likely to be workable and to reduce waste further from the 14.6% level of a year ago, lowering the $12.00 variable cost per unit.

Point 2: Involvement gives employees a voice despite the hierarchical, autocratic structure, raising motivation and commitment. Better engagement can help sustain the fall in defects from 5.1% to 2.8% and protect the 14,000-unit output needed to justify the $180,000 website and studio investment, while also supporting the 66% of customers who prefer sustainably made swimwear.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CBS's waste, defect rate and staffing.

questions.question_text: CBS needs a quality-control supervisor to tackle its 2.8% defect rate. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment. Which should CBS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal recruitment: Promoting an existing worker is cheap, quick and boosts morale because staff see a career path, which is valuable in a 30-person partnership. The candidate already knows CBS's products and processes, so can start reducing the 2.8% defect rate immediately and help drive fabric waste below 11.2%. The limitation is a smaller talent pool: the insert shows two staff lack quality-control training, so the best operator may still need $640-per-person external courses, and internal promotion can leave a gap in the original role.

External recruitment: Hiring from outside brings fresh quality-control expertise and new ideas for the new e-commerce range, which an in-house candidate may lack. It widens the pool beyond 30 staff and can introduce up-to-date inspection methods. Drawbacks are higher advertising and selection costs, a longer settling-in period, and the risk that an outsider does not fit the Cornwall shop culture or the autocratic leadership style, which could disrupt the team just as the $180,000 website launches.

Decision: CBS should choose internal recruitment, supported by quality-control training for the promoted worker. It is faster, cheaper and retains product knowledge while the 2.8% defect rate and 11.2% waste need urgent attention; external recruitment is rejected because the costs and induction delay are hard to justify for a partnership with $98,000 fixed costs, and the same $640 courses can build the needed skills in-house.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of internal and external recruitment with limited application to CBS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to CBS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods applied to CBS with a justified decision covering cost, speed and quality expertise.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CBS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $98,000 ÷ ($26.00 − $12.00) = $98,000 ÷ $14.00 = 7,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 7,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $26.00 − $12.00 = $14.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $14.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CBS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 7,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 14,000 units shows a margin of safety of 7,000 units, indicating how far sales could fall before the $180,000 website and studio cease to cover costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $14.00 lets managers test the $3 premium for sustainable swimwear: if the premium is accepted, contribution rises to $17.00, showing how the 66% of customers who prefer sustainable products could improve profit.
3. Fixed costs and contribution help judge whether trade credit of $90,000 can be serviced from the contribution on 14,000 units before more supplier finance is used.
4. Unit cost data ($98,000 ÷ 14,000 units + $12.00 = $19.00 a unit) enables monthly benchmarking, so managers can monitor the 11.2% fabric waste and 5.4-day delivery time as sources of avoidable cost.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 7,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $14.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 7,000 units versus 14,000-unit output; testing the $3 sustainable premium against $14.00 contribution; trade-credit servicing of $90,000; and unit-cost benchmarking at $19.00 to monitor 11.2% fabric waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CBS's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CBS's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.25 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $54,000 inventories + $36,000 trade receivables + $18,000 cash = $108,000; 2025 current assets = $45,000 + $48,000 + $27,000 = $120,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $108,000 ÷ $72,000 = 1.50; for 2025 it is $120,000 ÷ $60,000 = 2.00. The stricter 2024 measure is ($108,000 − $54,000) ÷ $72,000 = $54,000 ÷ $72,000 = 0.75; for 2025 it is ($120,000 − $45,000) ÷ $60,000 = $75,000 ÷ $60,000 = 1.25.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has strengthened markedly. The broader measure rose from 1.50 to 2.00 because current liabilities fell from $72,000 to $60,000 while current assets grew from $108,000 to $120,000. The stricter measure, which removes inventories, improved from 0.75 to 1.25, so CBS can now cover short-term debts without relying on swimwear stock — valuable when 11.2% of fabric is wasted and 5.4-day delivery times tie up working capital. The stronger evidence is the stricter measure, since its rise is not dependent on inventory that may not sell quickly out of season. Trade receivables did rise from $36,000 to $48,000, however, which could strains cash if shop or online customers pay late, and the partnership should monitor this as the $180,000 website investment begins.

Conclusion: CBS's liquidity has improved. Both the broader measure (1.50 to 2.00) and the stricter measure (0.75 to 1.25) show stronger short-term solvency without depending on stock. The residual concern is higher receivables, so Isla Corbin should tighten credit control before extending the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CBS of switching to sustainable fabric for its swimwear range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Sustainable fabric directly matches the survey finding that 66% of beachwear customers prefer responsibly made swimwear and 57% would pay $3 more. That premium would lift contribution per unit from $14.00 to $17.00 if accepted, helping cover fixed costs of $98,000 and supporting the $180,000 website investment, while also reducing the reputational damage of the 11.2% fabric waste.

Disadvantage: Sustainable materials usually cost more than conventional fabric, which would raise the $12.00 variable cost per unit and could offset the $3 premium if suppliers pass on the 11.3% input-cost inflation. If the fabric is harder to cut, the 11.2% waste rate and 2.8% defect rate could worsen, and the insert gives no evidence that all 14,000 units can be sold at the higher price, so the benefit is uncertain.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CBS's survey data, costs and waste.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.00%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in fabric input costs will affect CBS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.50% to 4.00%): CBS has no bank loan in the insert — its $180,000 expansion is funded by $90,000 trade credit and $90,000 retained profit — so there is no direct interest charge to recalculate. The effect is indirect: suppliers offering credit may face higher borrowing costs, and the 3.9% growth in seaside tourism spending could slow if households face dearer credit. Because the impact is second-order and the partnership has no loan exposure, this is the least damaging of the three changes.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.23 per hour): The insert states a workforce of 30 but no hours worked or pay rates, so a defensible annual wage total cannot be invented. The appropriate comparison is productivity — 14,000 units ÷ 30 staff = about 467 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is manageable; if the 5.4-day delivery time and 11.2% fabric waste absorb staff time, unit labour cost rises and the $14.00 contribution per unit is squeezed. Training the two staff lacking quality-control skills at $640 each would help protect productivity.

Fabric input-cost inflation (11.3%): The insert does not decompose the $12.00 variable cost, so only a labelled bound is honest: if the entire variable cost rose 11.3%, that adds 11.3% × $12.00 = $1.36 a unit; at 14,000 units this is about $19,040 a year (14,000 × $1.36). Even a partial increase cuts contribution on every unit, and the 11.2% waste rate means some fabric is discarded entirely. The $3 sustainable premium and 57% of customers willing to pay it offer a partial offset, but not enough to remove the threat.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in fabric input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every unit produced and directly erodes the $14.00 contribution that funds the $180,000 expansion, while the interest rise is indirect because CBS has no bank loan, and the wage effect can be mitigated if 467-unit productivity is maintained through training and waste reduction.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to CBS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CBS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to CBS with a well-justified judgement that fabric input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
